research.abstract: IntroductionAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) to first line antibiotics for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-attributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa. Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited settings is crucial. The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the genetic determinants of AMR. No study has explored whether human resistome composition in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes. This study will examine whether antibiotic treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisation. MethodsThis is an observational case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia). Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an antibiotic activity bioassay. Socio-demographic data, co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes will be recorded. AnalysisCross-sectional comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composition differs by pneumonia severity, antibiotic and healthcare exposure. Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composition over time. The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohens D = 0.505) change in the relative abundance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups. Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index), and relative abundance of ARG classes in the NPR. The primary objectives are to estimate the difference in diversity and relative abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia participants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia participants, and to investigate whether participants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR pattern. Ethics and disseminationThe study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Committee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Committee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076). Trial registration numberISRCTN64027792 STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDYO_ST_ABSStrengthsC_ST_ABSO_LIStudy design that uses metagenomic deep sequencing to enable direct, concurrent comparison of nasopharyngeal microbiome (NPM) and resistome (NPR) composition between community and hospitalised paediatric populations with pneumonia in a resource-limited setting. C_LIO_LIData on reported and urinary bioassay-detected antibiotic use prior to, and throughout the study, enabling detailed examination of antibiotic selective pressure on the NPR. C_LIO_LIInvestigation of the association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes from pneumonia. C_LI LimitationsO_LILimitations to this study include few sampling time points (two for community pneumonia and three for hospitalised pneumonia), which may not fully capture the impact of antibiotic exposure; the potential for residual confounding following adjustment for known potential confounders (e.g. age, sex, co-morbidities, household exposure to smoke and breastfeeding) in the association between resistome composition and adverse clinical outcomes, for which the authors have detailed statistical analysis measures; and ability to only determine association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes, rather than causal inference, due to the case-control study design. C_LI SUMMARYO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSThe nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance in children. Studies of nasopharyngeal microbiome composition have shown association with paediatric pneumonia severity and mortality. What this study addsThis study will describe nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) evolution under selective pressure of antibiotics and hospitalisation for paediatric pneumonia, and explore whether NPR composition is associated with health outcomes in a resource-limited setting. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis exploratory study could inform larger scale observational studies to examine the association between antibiotic resistance and health outcomes, by defining high-risk nasopharyngeal resistome composition, helping to determine the required sample size and contributing open-source bioinformatic pipelines. The study could also inform research for public health interventions, including antibiotic stewardship.

research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects the lungs and causes the disease tuberculosis, which the World Health Organization estimates causes 1 million deaths across the globe annually. Emergence of drug resistance has lessened the effectiveness and requires a longer duration of treatment. Bedaquiline was approved by the FDA in 2012 to treat multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis cases when no other treatment was viable. TBAJ-587, a derivative of Bedaquiline, has been found to be more effective at treating multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, and has fewer adverse effects. The aim of this project was to test if strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that have a mutation in Rv0678 causing overexpression of the MmpS5L5 efflux pump will evolve high-level resistance to TBAJ-587 at a higher frequency than wild-type strains. This was done by growing a wild-type M. tuberculosis strain and a ∆Rv0678 mutant on plates of 7H11 agar containing increasing concentrations of TBAJ-587, then selecting isolates and confirming resistance using an anti-microbial susceptibility assay to determine the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of the isolated strains. 72 strains from the wild-type background were assayed, and 114 from the ∆Rv0678 background were assayed. The resistant ∆Rv0678 strains tended to have higher minimum inhibitory concentrations that the resistant WT strains. Mutations in the WT strains were found throughout Rv0678, and D28, E6, A62 and I66 mutations in atpE, as well as L168 in atpB. Similar atpE mutations were found in ∆Rv0678, with the addition of mutations in A63 of atpE.

research.abstract: Background: Apolipoprotein B (apoB) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) are established biomarkers of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) that tend to be closely correlated. However, some individuals have discordant apoB and LDL-C. We evaluated whether apoB/LDL-C discordance is associated with elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), a key marker of systemic inflammation, in a nationally representative sample. Methods and Results: We analyzed 2226 adults aged 20 years or older from the 2015 to 2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete apoB, LDL-C, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). LDL-C and apoB were converted to survey-weighted scores, and discordance was the residual of apoB regressed on LDL-C. Participants were classified as apoBhigh, LDL-C-high, or concordant (reference). The association of discordance group with elevated hs-CRP (>3 mg/L) was estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes. Discordance was present in 26.4% of adults (13.7% apoBhigher, 12.6% LDL-C-higher). Elevated hs-CRP prevalence differed by discordance group: 47.6% (95% CI, 37.6?57.7) in the apoB-high group versus 20.5% (12.9?28.1) in the LDL-C-high group and 33.6% (29.7?37.4) in the concordant group. Relative to concordant participants, adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP were higher for apoB-high discordance (odds ratio [OR], 1.58; 95% CI, 1.03?2.45) and lower for LDL-C-high discordance (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.30?0.78). Similar results were obtained among participants not on statin therapy, with apoB-high discordance demonstrating stronger adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP (OR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01?4.04). Conclusion: Discordantly high apoB relative to LDL-C is associated with systemic inflammation in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.

research.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.

research.abstract: Abstract The ecological radiation of organisms in diverse light environments depends, in part, on adaptive alterations within visual systems, particularly retinal photoreceptors and their visual pigments. Evidence of visual adaptation occurs across vertebrate lineages but is notably lacking in turtles, despite their complex visual system with up to eight photoreceptor cell types and five visual pigments. This lack of knowledge is especially pronounced in side-neck turtles (Pleurodira), as nearly all information on turtle vision derives from hidden-neck turtles (Cryptodira). Here, we bridge this ∼200-million-year evolutionary gap by investigating visual opsin evolution using an eye transcriptome and whole-genome sequences from 59 turtle species spanning both suborders, as well as an additional 42 representative reptile species. We estimated selective pressures using codon-based evolutionary models, testing for positive selection and long-term shifts between turtles and other reptiles, between suborders, and among major habitat types. We also analysed spectral tuning sites to assess how spectral sensitivity diverged between and within suborders. Our analyses revealed remarkably conserved turtle visual opsin sequences, with phylogeny-wide positive selection detected only in LWS . Habitat explained more shifts in selective pressure than taxonomy, with long-term shifts detected across all five opsins. Spectral tuning sites predict conserved UV sensitivity of SWS1 across cryptodirans, consistent with the few species previously characterised, whereas shared changes identified in pleurodirans predict violet sensitivity, revealing previously unrecognized divergence in short-wavelength vision between turtle suborders. This study advances our understanding of turtle visual system evolution and highlights the need for conservation strategies that account for their distinct visual capabilities.

research.abstract: Background: Linkage of infectious-disease surveillance data to mortality records is important for estimating long-term outcomes, but incomplete personal identifiers present methodological challenges. We developed and validated a deterministic linkage framework for linking the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System (NTBS) with Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality records. Methods: TB notifications in England from 2001 to 2024 were linked to ONS mortality records using 12 sequential matching rules based on combinations of NHS number, date of birth, name, postcode, sex and phonetic matching. Linkage outputs underwent person level deduplication and clerical review. Precision and recall were estimated, and potential linkage bias assessed by variation in identifier completeness and linkage success. Confirmed false-positive links identified during validation were removed from the analytical dataset. Results: Among 151,965 TB notifications, 28,060 initial links were identified. Following deduplication, validation and refinement, 26,937 linked notifications were retained. Estimated precision increased from 97.7% to 99.2% (95% CI 96-100.0) following removal of false-positive links; estimated recall was 98.1% (95% CI 95.4-98.6%). More than 90% of links used NHS-number-based match keys. PDS enrichment increased NHS-number availability and enabled additional NHS-number-based links, although a small proportion linked to different ONS records following enrichment. NHS number availability and linkage success differed across demographic and social groups, demonstrating differential linkage. Conclusions: A hierarchical deterministic approach combined with targeted validation achieved high linkage accuracy while identifying and addressing differential linkage. This provides a transparent framework for future NTBS-ONS linkage and may be adaptable to other surveillance systems where comparable identifiers are available.

research.abstract: Background Anterior chest wall tuberculosis is an uncommon form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that can mimic a chronic pyogenic abscess or chest wall mass. Its indolent presentation and absence of constitutional symptoms may delay diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings. Case presentation A 22-year-old previously healthy male soldier presented with a progressively enlarging parasternal-xiphoid swelling and intermittent seropurulent discharge, without respiratory or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed a minimally tender 5 × 2 cm fluctuant swelling with a draining sinus and localized skin changes. Thoracic computed tomography showed a 57 × 18 mm subcutaneous collection at the xiphoid level without demonstrated pleural or osseous involvement, alongside centrilobular nodules and a tree-in-bud pattern suggestive of pulmonary infection. Incision, drainage, and debridement were performed. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing of a fluid specimen detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex at a low bacillary load, without rifampicin resistance detected. Histopathological examination was reported to show caseating granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Sputum testing was also positive for M. tuberculosis, supporting concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis. First-line antituberculous therapy was initiated. The wound was closed at the 14-day postoperative assessment. Following six months of treatment, the patient remained asymptomatic; follow-up computed tomography demonstrated resolution of the chest wall collection and regression of pulmonary abnormalities. Conclusion Chest wall tuberculosis should be considered in patients with persistent parasternal swelling or a draining sinus, even without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Tissue sampling, molecular and histopathological evaluation, and assessment for concomitant pulmonary disease support timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis withstands acidic conditions to survive and replicate within macrophages. To define the genetic determinants of this adaptation, we performed a transposon screen in a lipid-rich, acidic medium that mimics the host environment and supports robust M. tuberculosis growth. This screen identified ldtB , encoding an L,D-transpeptidase, as essential for growth and survival under acid stress. Loss of LdtB decreased 3–3 peptidoglycan cross-linking, disrupted cell wall architecture, and impaired intrabacterial pH homeostasis, resulting in increased susceptibility to cell wall–active antibiotics. Notably, M. tuberculosis lacking LdtB displayed heightened sensitivity to meropenem within macrophages, suggesting that targeting this enzyme could potentiate β-lactam efficacy during infection. These findings establish LdtB as a key mediator linking peptidoglycan homeostasis to acid stress resistance and underscores the importance of in vitro culture models that recapitulate the host microenvironment for uncovering new in vivo active therapeutic targets. Teaser Disabling a key peptidoglycan cross-linking enzyme compromises M. tuberculosis survival under acidic stress and antibiotic exposure.

research.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased in several high-income countries since 2020. Proposed explanations include pandemic related disruption of treatment for latent tuberculosis, changes in population composition, and immune dysfunction following SARS CoV 2 infection. We assessed whether TB presentations increased during the pandemic era and then tested whether community SARS CoV 2 activity was followed by increased mycobacterial disease. Methods: We conducted a population-based ecological time-series study of first TB- and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM)-coded hospital, emergency-department and ambulatory clinic presentations in the Greater Toronto/Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+), Ontario (2024 population approximately 11.2 million), from April 2011 through March 2024. NTM served as a comparator because it shares diagnostic pathways with TB but differs epidemiologically. Negative binomial projection and full-series models estimated pandemic-era changes under three alternative trend assumptions. Distributed lag non linear models estimated cumulative rate ratios for standardized community viral activity over 0 to 12 weeks; sensitivity analyses extended the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks. Influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were prespecified comparators; data for five additional viral exposures were obtained after the primary analysis was completed and analysed as exploratory comparisons. Results: We identified 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded acute-care presentations. Across six models, estimated pandemic-era TB increases ranged from 3% to 22%. No model suggested an increased in NTM. SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with TB (cumulative rate ratio per 1-SD increase over 0 to 12 weeks 0.909, 95% CI 0.822 to 1.006) or NTM (0.953, 0.868 to 1.047). No positive associations were identified in subgroup analyses or with maximum lags of 26 or 52 weeks. Influenza was not associated with either outcome. RSV was associated with TB and NTM; only the RSV/NTM association met the Bonferroni threshold among the prespecified comparisons, and no exploratory associations met the experiment wide threshold. Conclusions: We identified a modest pandemic era increase in TB-coded acute-care presentations in Ontario, Canada, although its estimated size depended on assumptions about underlying trends. NTM-coded presentations did not increase. Community SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with subsequent TB or NTM presentations at lags of up to one year and did not provide a temporal explanation for the population-level TB increase. Individual-level effects cannot be excluded.

research.abstract: Abstract Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types – including insertions and deletions – within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT The Brown Swiss ( BS ) cattle breed is one of the major Swiss dairy breeds. Intensive selection and the widespread use of few elite sires in artificial insemination have increased inbreeding and the occurrence of deleterious recessive alleles in the homozygous state. Analyzing life trajectories in large, genotyped cohorts can identify hidden recessive disorders that are difficult to detect using traditional case-control association testing. Long-read DNA sequencing enables precise detection of causal alleles, including structural variants. This study aimed to (1) identify cryptic recessive loci affecting rearing performance in Swiss BS cattle, (2) evaluate their impact on survival, (3) characterize the associated phenotype, (4) identify the causal variant using long-read whole-genome sequencing, and (5) assess its functional impact. Using Homozygous Haplotype Enrichment/Depletion ( HHED ) mapping, we identified a risk haplotype ( BH39 ) on chromosome 15 spanning from 16,276,819 bp to 16,446,984 bp that was associated with increased juvenile mortality within the first 180 days of life when present in the homozygous state. The BH39 occurred at a frequency of approximately 4.5% in Swiss BS cattle and 5.3% in German and Austrian BS cattle, and homozygous carriers exhibited a significantly reduced first-year survival rate. Five females homozygous for BH39 underwent clinical examination. They all showed recurrent respiratory disease, impaired growth, poor body condition, rough hair coat, and brown-discolored teeth. Pathological examination revealed bronchopneumonia and eosinophilic enteritis. Clinicopathological findings indicated failure to thrive and immunodeficiency. Long-read WGS of two BH39 homozygous calves revealed a private homozygous coding variant that was in high linkage disequilibrium with BH39. The identified structural variant was an insertion of a large transposable element (10.4 kb ERVK[2-1-LTR]) into the third exon of ALKBH8 (NM_001080341.2 c.267_268indel). Full-length RNA sequencing of cerebellum and liver from a homozygous calf revealed that the endogenous retrovirus ( ERV ) insertion introduces a cryptic transcription termination signal, truncating ALKBH8 mRNA. This study demonstrates that exploring population-scale genomic data and mining thousands of life-history records, followed by veterinary follow-up evaluations and molecular genetic analyses, provides an effective strategy for identifying cryptic recessive disorders that shorten the lifespan of cattle. The findings provide strong evidence that the ERV insertion into the coding sequence of ALKBH8 represents a loss-of-function variant that causes a previously undescribed recessive disorder that results in increased rearing loss. Interpretive summary We identified a recessive disorder in Brown Swiss cattle that causes retarded growth, recurrent infections, immunodeficiency, and increased mortality during the first year of life. Using population-scale genomic data, clinical investigations, and long-read sequencing, we linked the disorder to an exonic transposable element insertion disrupting ALKBH8 . The identification of the causal variant now enables direct genetic testing and the implementation of genome-based mating strategies to avoid carrier-by-carrier matings and, consequently, prevent the birth of affected homozygous offspring. We demonstrate the utility of integrating large-scale breeding records, veterinary phenotyping, and advanced genomics to identify hidden defects affecting livestock health and productivity.

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.

research.abstract: Polygonatum zanlanscianense Pamp. is a perennial herb (Asparagaceae) endemic to China, whose rhizomes are used in folk medicine as a substitute for Polygonati Rhizoma. Although its plastome has been reported, the mitogenome remained uncharacterized. Here, we assembled and annotated the complete linear mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense and analysed its gene repertoire, codon usage, repeats, RNA editing sites, MTPTs, synteny, phylogeny and Ka/Ks. The 689,491-bp mitogenome (GC 46.23%) encodes 56 genes: 36 PCGs, three rRNA genes and 17 tRNA genes. Codon usage is biased toward A/U-ending codons. We identified 68 SSRs, 25 tandem repeats, 1366 dispersed repeat pairs, 585 predicted C-to-U editing sites concentrated at the first and second codon positions, and 30 MTPT fragments accounting for 2.24% of the mitogenome. Phylogenetic analysis placed P. zanlanscianense as sister to Polygonatum kingianum Collett & Hemsl. Median Ka/Ks was below 1 for 33 of the 35 genes analysed; although rpl5 and ccmB showed elevated ratios, branch-site tests did not support positive selection. This first mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense provides genomic resources for comparative genomic, phylogenetic and medicinal studies in Polygonatum.

research.abstract: Abstract Blood-based biomarkers are transforming Alzheimer’s disease (AD) detection, with plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p-tau217) being a leading candidate. However, circulating p-tau217 originates from both central nervous system (CNS) and non-CNS sources, limiting specificity. Here, we benchmark the performance of next-generation p-tau217 biomarkers that are selective for p-tau217 from predominantly CNS origin versus the conventional non-selective p-tau217. Across neuropathologically-defined, Aβ- and tau-neuroimaging–characterized, and memory clinic cohorts, plasma brain-derived-p-tau217 (BD-p-tau217)–either alone or in ratio with brain-derived tau expressed as a percentage (BD-p-tau217%)–identified AD pathology and clinical AD with larger effect sizes, higher discriminative accuracies, and improved sensitivity and specificity, outperforming conventional alternatives. Furthermore, BD-p-tau217% and BD-p-tau217 demonstrated more robust prediction of future clinical progression up to two decades later. Importantly, diagnostic performance remained high in older adults with diabetes and cardiovascular disease, populations in which standard p-tau217 showed reduced specificity. The findings were independently replicated in a large multicenter cohort, demonstrating the robustness and generalizability of the observed improvements across clinical, imaging, and longitudinal outcomes. These results establish plasma BD-p-tau217% and BD-p-tau217 as biologically grounded and clinically robust biomarkers that advance early detection, diagnosis and prognosis of AD. One Sentence Summary Plasma brain-derived p-tau217 and its ratio over brain-derived tau improve the specificity of the leading blood-based Alzheimer’s disease biomarker p-tau217.

research.abstract: Background: Cardiac sympathetic denervation varies in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Our previous neuropathological study demonstrated an association between greater Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and milder cardiac sympathetic denervation in DLB. We investigated whether medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA), a potential marker of concomitant AD pathology, correlates with cardiac sympathetic denervation assessed by 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy in probable DLB. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, we analyzed 162 patients with probable DLB. MTA was assessed by Voxel-based Specific Regional Analysis System for Alzheimer's Disease (VSRAD) Z-scores, and cardiac MIBG uptake by early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios. Associations were examined using Spearman and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and disease duration. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with MIBG-dependent classification, diabetes mellitus or cardiac disease. Results: VSRAD Z-scores correlated positively with early ({rho} = 0.173, P = 0.028) and delayed H/M ratios ({rho} = 0.225, P = 0.004). After adjustment, the association was no longer significant for the early H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.133, P = 0.094), whereas it remained significant for the delayed H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.196, P = 0.013). The adjusted delayed H/M association persisted after excluding 18 patients with MIBG-dependent classification ({rho} = 0.211, P = 0.012) and 40 with diabetes or cardiac disease ({rho} = 0.231, P = 0.011). Conclusions: Greater MTA was associated with relatively preserved cardiac MIBG uptake in probable DLB, particularly on delayed imaging. Consistent with our neuropathological observations, these findings suggest that concomitant AD pathology may contribute to variability in cardiac sympathetic denervation.

research.abstract: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is a common psychiatric condition characterized by a consistent fear of social evaluation. Despite heritability estimates of up to 69%, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of SAD remain limited relative to other psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, the contribution of environmental factors, particularly rural versus urban residence, to SAD risk is poorly characterized. Using the All of Us dataset (N=414,830, Ncases=10,918), our aims were to: (1) identify genetic risk loci for SAD through within-ancestry GWAS (N=1,467—222,500), cross-ancestry meta-analysis, and a European-ancestry meta-analysis (N =788,384); (2) further characterize the genetic architecture of SAD through polygenic risk score (PRS), phenome-wide association (PheWAS), laboratory-wide association (LabWAS), and genetic correlation; and (3) stratify all analyses by rural and urban environment. Across all ancestries examined, rural residence was associated with increased odds of SAD (OR=1.42, 95%; CI (1.36-1.50); p<5×10 -8 ). Although no genome-wide significant loci were identified, several loci reached suggestive significance, notably an intronic variant in NEGR1 (rs12065683), a gene with prior associations to anxiety and neurodevelopmental disorders. PheWAS analyses identified ear disorders as the most nominally significant phenotype (p=3.76x10 -5 ; OR=1.45) and significant associations with lymphocyte count were identified in the LabWAS (p=1.80x10 -5 ). These findings provide further insight into the genetic architecture of SAD and suggest that residential environment may modify risk. Larger-scale genetic studies will be required to validate the observed suggestive loci and gene x environment interaction models to form conclusions regarding the true effect of residence.

research.abstract: Abstract Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae , which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae , supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus “Vandarnavirus” proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate “Vandarnavirus” genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences. Importance Freshwater ecosystems support primary production and nutrient cycling, but their associated RNA-virus diversity remains incompletely characterized. Here, metatranscriptomics recovered diverse viral sequences from five Finnish freshwater sites and one exploratory marine sample from Hiroshima Bay, Japan. Two marnavirus-like vOTUs were detected only in the Vantaanjoki river sample and formed a distinct RdRp lineage outside currently recognized Marnaviridae genera. We provisionally propose the candidate genus “Vandarnavirus”; formal taxonomic placement and host associations require further evaluation. By connecting freshwater viral discovery with genome architecture and phylogeny, this work expands the known ecological range of marnavirus-like viruses and highlights freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgal viruses.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica , a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis , a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica , reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ∼275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

research.abstract: Purpose Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. Methods We performed systematic searches in seven databases until July 2026. We included observational studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the TB score to diagnosis of TB across different clinical contexts. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Meta-analysis was performed using the logit function, and GRADE was employed to assess certainty of evidence (CoE). Results Twenty-eight studies were included. For distinguishing pulmonary TB from other respiratory diseases, the TB score showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84) and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64-0.78), respectively, with an AUC of 0.82. When comparing pulmonary TB to healthy controls, sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity was 0.86, with an AUC of 0.87. Performance was lower for meningeal tuberculosis (sensitivity 0.58; specificity 0.67) and for distinguishing active from latent TB (sensitivity 0.73; specificity 0.76). Risk of bias was generally low. The CoE for most outcomes was very low. Conclusion The TB score shows moderate diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary TB, with pooled sensitivity below the WHO TPP minimum for a standalone triage test. High heterogeneity and very low CoE limit confidence in these findings. Its potential role as a complementary tool remains investigational and requires validation in prospective studies.

research.abstract: Physical activity levels are increasingly investigated as candidate digital biomarkers across a range of psychiatric and neurological disorders. Physical activity is heritable, with associated genetic variants implicating genes expressed in the central nervous system. However, its shared genetic architecture with disorders such as schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease (PD) remains poorly understood. Here, we applied complementary genome-wide methods to investigate the genetic overlap between physical activity and these disorders. We used a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of objectively measured physical activity (n = 89,683), enhanced through multi-trait GWAS incorporating self-reported activity measures (n = 124,842-377,234). In cross-trait analysis with recent GWAS of schizophrenia (n = 53,386 cases, 77,258 controls) and PD (63,555 cases, 17,700 proxy cases, and 1,746,386 controls), we find that while genetic correlations are negligible (rg=-0.02-0.02, p>0.05), polygenic overlap was substantial, with the majority of trait-influencing variants shared between the three traits. This contrast reflects mixed effect directions, which we show through convergent results from causal mixture modelling, local genetic correlations, and conjunctional false discovery rate analysis. Genes shared between activity and schizophrenia were differentially expressed in the amygdala and several basal ganglia structures, and associated with a range of cognitive-affective traits. In contrast, genes shared between activity and PD were largely associated with neurodegenerative disorders and structural brain phenotypes. Together, these findings suggest that activity draws on genes involved in motor, cognitive, affective and neurodegenerative processes, providing a genetic basis for its alteration across diverse neuropsychiatric disorders.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Species inhabiting high-elevation environments face energetic and physiological challenges, creating opportunities for adaptive divergence from lowland taxa. The yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), a Critically Endangered primate endemic to high-elevation forests in Andean Perú, provides a unique system for investigating the evolutionary consequences of long-term occupation of high elevations. We used Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) to generate a high-coverage mitochondrial reference genome using low-quality fecal samples. Using this and a new mitogenome from a closely-related lowland common woolly monkey (L. lagotricha poeppigii), we estimated divergence dates and calculated substitution ratios to investigate the evolutionary history of both Lagothrix taxa and assess whether high-elevation living has left signatures of selection in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes of L. flavicauda. RESULTS: We assembled a high-coverage (9190X) reference mitogenome of 16,603 bp for L. flavicauda from a 15-year-old fecal sample, and a novel mitogenome for L. lagotricha poeppigii from fresh tissue (112X, 16,590 bp). Our phylogenetic reconstruction is consistent with other platyrrhine primate phylogenies with high bootstrap support, with the two Lagothrix taxa showing evidence of having diverged from one another ~ 2.8 million years ago. Substitution (d N /d S) ratios suggest purifying selection on protein-coding mitogenomic regions in all assessed lineages. CONCLUSIONS: We found no evidence of positive selection acting on mitochondrial protein-coding genes in either L. flavicauda or the broader genus Lagothrix; all analyses instead support pervasive purifying selection across genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. These results suggest that unlike in some other non-human primates occupying high elevations, the adaptive response of L. flavicauda to living in the Andes does not appear to involve evolution in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathway, and likely involves alternative genetic pathways or mechanisms not captured by mitochondrial sequence evolution. By providing the first publicly available high-coverage mitochondrial genome for L. flavicauda, this study establishes a foundation for future population mitogenomic investigations of adaptation, evolutionary history, and conservation in this Critically Endangered, high-altitude primate.

research.abstract: Abstract Chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs) are key drivers of tumor evolution, disease progression and therapeutic resistance, and their identification is critical for delineating tumor clonal structure. However, accurately detecting CNAs from single-cell data remains challenging as most existing CNA callers still analyze a single omics layer and are susceptible to assay-specific noise. Recently, single-cell multi-omics techniques have enabled joint sequencing of multiple molecular layers (e.g., genomics and transcriptomics) simultaneously in the same cells, yet computational methods that fully exploit such complementary multi-omics data for CNA analysis remain limited. Here, we present MintCNA, a unified framework for CNA detection from paired single-cell multi-omics data. MintCNA integrates deep-learning based denoising with a missingness-adjusted multivariate change-point detection procedure to enhance CNA profiling across omics layers. In simulations, MintCNA outperformed existing single-cell CNA callers across all evaluated scenarios. MintCNA showed the highest correlation with bulk whole-genome sequencing in a colorectal cancer dataset and revealed progressive loss of chromosome 17 during metastasis. In an IDH-mutant glioma cohort, MintCNA generalized to paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data and identified copy number subclones corresponding to distinct malignant cell states. MintCNA provides an advanced multi-omics integrative single-cell CNA analysis tool for better delineating the mechanisms underlying disease progression and tumor evolution.

research.abstract: Abstract Glutamate links cellular metabolism with excitatory neurotransmission, yet the evolutionary histories of its metabolic enzymes, transporters, and receptor paralogues have not been compared within a common human-reference-anchored phylogenomic framework. Here, we traced human UniProt/Swiss-Prot-associated protein lineages across 89 eukaryotic proteomes using homology searches, sequence and domain filtering, maximum-likelihood phylogenies assessed with transfer bootstrap expectation (TBE) and ultrafast bootstrap (UFBoot), sequence-stability analyses, and GeneRax gene-tree/species-tree reconciliation under a duplication–loss model. Metabolic enzyme homologues showed the broadest distributions: GLUD, GOT, and GPT were recovered across multiple eukaryotic supergroups, whereas GLS-associated sequences were detected in metazoans and the ichthyosporean Capsaspora owczarzaki . SLC17 and SLC1 transporter homologues were recovered only from sampled metazoans. Receptor distributions varied among families: GRM and GRIN sequences were detected across sampled cnidarians and bilaterians, GRIA and GRIK across bilaterian groups, and GRID only in seven sampled vertebrate species. Reconciliation mapped numerous paralogue-associated duplications to early vertebrate, gnathostome, and osteichthyan ancestral nodes, alongside independent lineage-specific expansions. Although many local phylogenetic relationships were supported, deeper relationships in some transporter and receptor families remained uncertain, with TBE and UFBoot providing different support values. These findings characterize the human-associated glutamatergic repertoire as an evolutionary mosaic of gene families with distinct taxonomic distributions and duplication histories. Because homology searches were anchored on human reference proteins, the inferred distributions represent detectable lineages in the sampled dataset rather than definitive evidence of gene-family origins or absence.
